claims.text: Conventional stainless steel relies on a naturally formed passive oxide layer.
The native passive oxide layer of conventional stainless steel is insufficient in extreme corrosive environments.
Laser cladding can deposit a multicomponent protective coating on steel.
A predictive data-driven or machine-learning model can identify the optimal coating formulation and laser-cladding parameters.
An optimized laser-clad coating will significantly enhance the corrosion resistance of stainless steel under extreme corrosive conditions.
The laser-cladding treatment can preserve the underlying bulk properties of stainless steel.
Changing the multicomponent coating composition can refine the laser-clad coating microstructure.
Changing coating composition can control the phases present in a laser-clad coating.
The engineered coating promotes formation of a stable, self-healing passive oxide layer.
The engineered coating may contain additional protective phases.
A refined grain structure and controlled phase composition enhance passivation and reduce corrosion attack.
The optimized laser-clad coating will have a significantly lower corrosion rate than stainless steel protected only by its native oxide.
The optimized laser-clad coating will provide higher surface hardness than the native stainless-steel surface.
Corrosion improvement is conditional on the coating remaining intact.
Corrosion improvement is expected only within the environmental ranges used to optimize the model.
Excessively severe exposure or adverse effects of cladding on the bulk material may eliminate the improvement.
The magnitude of corrosion-resistance improvement and the optimal formulation depend on experimental validation and the particular corrosive environment.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and predicted outcome define the comparator as stainless steel with only its native passive oxide, whereas the experiment specifies a control receiving a conventional surface treatment. These may not be equivalent comparators.
